statement: Let $f$ be [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) on an [open set](c:open-set) $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$, that is, complex differentiable at every point, with no continuity assumed for $f'$. Then for every closed solid [triangle](c:triangle) $T \subset U$ the [contour integral](c:contour-integral) $\oint_{\partial T} f(z)\,dz$ is zero.

hypotheses.text: The set $U \subseteq \mathbb{C}$ is [open](c:open-set) and contains the closed solid triangle $T$.
The function $f$ is complex differentiable at every point of $U$.

conclusion: The integral of $f$ around the boundary of $T$ is $0$.

proofs.name: Goursat subdivision
proofs.slogan: Quarter the triangle again and again, keep the worst quarter, and beat its integral with the linear approximation of $f$ at the limit point.
proofs.scope: Every closed solid triangle in $U$; for a degenerate triangle the boundary integral is $0$ directly. Cauchy's theorem on discs follows from this case through a primitive, which this proof does not cover.

roles.why: The set $U$ holds $T$, so the limit point $z_0$ of the nested triangles is a point where $f$ is differentiable.
Differentiability at $z_0$ gives the linear approximation with an error that is small compared with $|z - z_0|$.

steps.slogan: Split $T$ into four triangles by joining the midpoints of its sides.
steps.detail: The four triangles have half the diameter $d$ and half the perimeter $p$ of $T$. Their boundary integrals add up to $\oint_{\partial T} f$, because each inner edge is traversed twice in opposite directions, so one of them, $T_1$, has $|\oint_{\partial T_1} f| \ge \frac14 |\oint_{\partial T} f|$.

steps.slogan: Repeat the split to get nested triangles $T_n$ of shrinking size.
steps.detail: Induction gives $T \supseteq T_1 \supseteq T_2 \supseteq \cdots$ with diameter $2^{-n}d$, perimeter $2^{-n}p$ and $|\oint_{\partial T_n} f| \ge 4^{-n}|\oint_{\partial T} f|$.

steps.slogan: Take the common point $z_0$ of the nested [compact](c:compact-space) triangles.
steps.detail: The triangles are nonempty, compact and nested, and their diameters tend to $0$, so they meet in exactly one point $z_0 \in T \subset U$.

steps.slogan: Remove the linear part of $f$ at $z_0$, because it has a primitive.
steps.detail: Write $f(z) = f(z_0) + f'(z_0)(z - z_0) + \psi(z)(z - z_0)$ with $\psi(z) \to 0$ as $z \to z_0$. The linear part is the derivative of a polynomial, so its integral over the closed path $\partial T_n$ is $0$, and $|\oint_{\partial T_n} f| \le 2^{-n}p \cdot 2^{-n}d \cdot \sup_{T_n}|\psi|$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two bounds and let $n$ tend to infinity.
steps.detail: Steps 2 and 4 give $|\oint_{\partial T} f| \le 4^n \cdot 4^{-n} p d \sup_{T_n}|\psi| = p d \sup_{T_n}|\psi|$. The right side tends to $0$ because $T_n$ shrinks to $z_0$, so the integral is $0$.

concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Complex differentiability at one point gives the linear approximation there.
concepts.c:open-set: The open set holds the triangle and the limit point.
concepts.c:triangle: A triangle splits into four half-size triangles with cancelling inner edges.
concepts.c:contour-integral: The boundary integral is additive over the four sub-triangles.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness of the nested triangles gives their common point.

source.note: Goursat's subdivision proof (1900), as in Stein and Shakarchi, Complex Analysis, chapter 2, theorem 1.1.

statement:
Let $T$ be a [consistent](c:consistent-theory) [formal system](c:formal-system) whose set of axioms is [decidable](c:decidability) and which proves the axioms of [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic). (1) Some arithmetic sentence $R$ has $T 
vdash R$ and $T 
vdash 
eg R$. (2) If $T$ contains [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic), then $T$ does not prove the sentence $\mathrm{Con}(T)$ that expresses its consistency.

hypotheses.text: The theory $T$ is [consistent](c:consistent-theory): it proves no sentence together with its negation.
The set of axioms of $T$ is [decidable](c:decidability).
The theory $T$ proves the axioms of [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) $Q$.
For part (2), $T$ contains the axioms of [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic).

conclusion: $T$ is incomplete, and under the hypothesis of part (2) it does not prove $\mathrm{Con}(T)$.

proofs.name: Self-referential sentences
proofs.slogan: Code proofs by numbers, build sentences that speak about their own provability, and formalize the first argument inside the theory.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof: the representability of the proof relation (step 1) and the derivability conditions (step 5) rest on the cited work. Part (1) needs only consistency through Rosser's sentence, and part (2) needs the extra hypothesis.

roles.why: A decidable axiom set makes the proof relation decidable, so arithmetic can express it.
[Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) represents every decidable relation and proves the diagonal lemma.
Consistency excludes a proof of $G$, of Rosser's sentence or its negation, and of $\mathrm{Con}(T)$.
[Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) proves the derivability conditions that formalize step 3 inside $T$.

steps.slogan: Code formulas and proofs by numbers and express provability in arithmetic.
steps.detail: A [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering) assigns a number $\ulcorner\varphi\urcorner$ to each formula and each finite list of formulas. Because the axioms are decidable, the relation $\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, n)$, that $p$ codes a $T$-proof of the formula with code $n$, is decidable and so is represented in $Q$. Let $\mathrm{Prov}_T(x) = \exists p\,\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, x)$ be the [provability predicate](c:provability-predicate).

steps.slogan: Build the Gödel sentence $G$ that states its own unprovability.
steps.detail: For every formula $\varphi(x)$ the diagonal lemma gives a sentence $\sigma$ with $Q \vdash \sigma \leftrightarrow \varphi(\ulcorner\sigma\urcorner)$. With $\varphi = \neg\mathrm{Prov}_T$ it gives $G$ with $Q \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the consistent theory $T$ does not prove $G$.
steps.detail: If $T \vdash G$ with a proof of code $p$, then $Q$ proves the true numerical instance $\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner G\urcorner)$, so $T \vdash \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$ and step 2 gives $T \vdash \neg G$. This contradicts consistency, so $T \nvdash G$.

steps.slogan: Replace $G$ by Rosser's sentence to make its negation unprovable as well.
steps.detail:
The diagonal lemma gives $R$ with $Q \vdash R \leftrightarrow  orall p\,(\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner R\urcorner) 	o \exists q < p\ \mathrm{Prf}_T(q, \ulcorner
eg R\urcorner))$. A proof of $R$ or of $
eg R$ with code $p$ lets $Q$ check all codes below $p$, and in both cases $T$ proves both $R$ and $
eg R$, against consistency.

steps.slogan: Formalize step 3 inside $T$ to prove $\mathrm{Con}(T) \to G$.
steps.detail: With Peano arithmetic, $T$ proves the Hilbert-Bernays-Löb derivability conditions for $\mathrm{Prov}_T$. They turn step 3 into a proof in $T$ of $\mathrm{Con}(T) \to \neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$, which is $\mathrm{Con}(T) \to G$ by step 2.

steps.slogan: Combine Rosser's sentence and the formalized implication into the two parts.
steps.detail: Step 4 gives part (1). If $T \vdash \mathrm{Con}(T)$, then step 5 gives $T \vdash G$, which step 3 excludes, so $T \nvdash \mathrm{Con}(T)$ and part (2) holds.

concepts.c:consistent-theory: Consistency is what each contradiction argument breaks.
concepts.c:formal-system: The theorem limits a formal system whose proofs can be checked mechanically.
concepts.c:decidability: Decidable axioms make the proof relation expressible in arithmetic.
concepts.c:robinson-arithmetic: This weak base theory represents decidable relations and proves the diagonal lemma.
concepts.c:peano-arithmetic: Peano arithmetic proves the derivability conditions used for part (2).
concepts.c:godel-numbering: Numbering formulas lets arithmetic sentences talk about proofs.
concepts.c:provability-predicate: The diagonal sentences refer to this provability formula.

source.ref: C. Smoryński, The incompleteness theorems, in J. Barwise (ed.), Handbook of Mathematical Logic, North-Holland, Amsterdam, 1977, 821-865
source.note: Complete proofs of both theorems with the derivability conditions. The first theorem is from K. Gödel, Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 38 (1931), 173-198 (https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01700692), and the consistency-only form from J. B. Rosser, Journal of Symbolic Logic 1 (1936), 87-91.

statement: For $F \in L^2(\mathbb{R})$ with [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\hat F$, these are equivalent: (a) $F$ is the $L^2$ limit, as $y \to 0^+$, of $G(\cdot + iy)$ for a [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) $G$ on the [upper half-plane](c:upper-half-plane) with $\sup_{y>0}\int |G(x+iy)|^2\,dx < \infty$; (b) $\operatorname{Im} F$ is the [Hilbert transform](c:hilbert-transform) of $\operatorname{Re} F$; (c) $\hat F = 0$ almost everywhere on $(-\infty, 0)$.

hypotheses.text: The function $F\colon \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{C}$ is [square integrable](c:square-integrable-function).

conclusion: Conditions (a), (b) and (c) are equivalent: $F$ is the boundary value of a [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) function exactly when its imaginary part is the Hilbert transform of its real part.

proofs.name: Fourier support and Paley-Wiener
proofs.slogan: Translate each condition into the vanishing of $\hat F$ on negative frequencies, by the multiplier of $H$ and by the Paley-Wiener argument.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, with $\hat F(\xi) = \int F(x) e^{-2\pi i x\xi}\,dx$ and $H$ given on $L^2$ by the principal value integral with kernel $1/(\pi x)$. The function $F = 0$ satisfies all three conditions.

roles.why: Square integrability makes the [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) an isometry of $L^2$ by Plancherel, which every step uses.

steps.slogan: Write the [Hilbert transform](c:hilbert-transform) as the Fourier multiplier $-i\,\operatorname{sgn}\xi$.
steps.detail: The principal value kernel $1/(\pi x)$ has Fourier transform $-i\,\operatorname{sgn}\xi$, so $\widehat{Hu} = -i\,\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)\,\hat u$ for $u \in L^2$. Hence $H$ is an isometry of $L^2$ that maps real functions to real functions.

steps.slogan: Show that (b) and (c) are the same condition on $\hat F$.
steps.detail: Write $F = u + iv$ with $u, v$ real. If $v = Hu$, then $\hat F = (1 + \operatorname{sgn}\xi)\hat u$ vanishes for $\xi < 0$; conversely, (c) gives $HF = -iF$, and the real parts of $Hu + iHv = v - iu$ give $Hu = v$.

steps.slogan: Build $G$ from (c) as a Fourier integral over positive frequencies.
steps.detail: Set $G(z) = \int_0^\infty \hat F(\xi) e^{2\pi i z\xi}\,d\xi$ for $\operatorname{Im} z > 0$; it is [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) because $e^{-2\pi y\xi}$ is square integrable on $(0, \infty)$. Plancherel gives $\int |G(x+iy)|^2 dx = \int_0^\infty |\hat F|^2 e^{-4\pi y\xi} d\xi \le \|F\|^2$, and dominated convergence gives $G(\cdot + iy) \to F$ in $L^2$.

steps.slogan: Show from (a) that $\widehat{G_y}(\xi) = e^{-2\pi y\xi} g(\xi)$ for one function $g$.
steps.detail: Here $G_y = G(\cdot + iy)$. Cauchy's theorem for $G(z)e^{-2\pi i z\xi}$ on rectangles $[-A, A] \times [y_1, y_2]$, whose vertical sides contribute $0$ along a sequence $A \to \infty$ by the uniform $L^2$ bound, gives $e^{2\pi y_1\xi}\widehat{G_{y_1}} = e^{2\pi y_2\xi}\widehat{G_{y_2}}$ almost everywhere.

steps.slogan: Force $g = 0$ on negative frequencies by the uniform bound, then let $y \to 0$.
steps.detail: Plancherel gives $\int |g(\xi)|^2 e^{-4\pi y\xi}\,d\xi = \|G_y\|^2 \le C$ for all $y > 0$, and for $\xi < 0$ the weight grows to $\infty$ as $y \to \infty$, so monotone convergence forces $g = 0$ there. Since $G_y \to F$ in $L^2$, $\hat F = \lim_{y \to 0} e^{-2\pi y\xi} g$ also vanishes on $(-\infty, 0)$.

steps.slogan: Chain the implications into the equivalence of (a), (b) and (c).
steps.detail: Step 2 gives (b) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c), step 3 gives (c) $\Rightarrow$ (a), and steps 4 and 5 give (a) $\Rightarrow$ (c). So the three conditions are equivalent.

concepts.c:fourier-transform: Every condition becomes a statement about the support of $\hat F$.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of the extension allows the contour shifts of step 4.
concepts.c:upper-half-plane: On the upper half-plane $e^{2\pi i z\xi}$ decays for $\xi > 0$.
concepts.c:hilbert-transform: Its multiplier $-i\,\operatorname{sgn}\xi$ links condition (b) to the frequency support.
concepts.c:square-integrable-function: Square integrability allows Plancherel's isometry for all functions involved.
concepts.c:hardy-space: Condition (a) says that $G$ lies in the Hardy space $H^2$.

source.note: The classical proof through the Paley-Wiener theorem for the Hardy space H^2, as in Titchmarsh, Introduction to the Theory of Fourier Integrals (1937), and Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, chapter 19.

statement: Let $n \ge 2$ and let $X$ be an $(n-1)$-[connected](c:n-connected-space) space. Then the reduced [homology](c:homology) groups $\tilde H_k(X;\mathbb{Z})$ vanish for $k < n$, and the Hurewicz map $h\colon \pi_n(X) \to H_n(X;\mathbb{Z})$ on the $n$-th [homotopy group](c:homotopy-group), which sends the class of $\alpha\colon S^n \to X$ to $\alpha_*[S^n]$, is an isomorphism.

hypotheses.text: The degree satisfies $n \ge 2$.
The space $X$ is $(n-1)$-[connected](c:n-connected-space): it is path-connected and $\pi_k(X) = 0$ for $1 \le k \le n-1$.

conclusion: $\tilde H_k(X) = 0$ for $k < n$, and $h\colon \pi_n(X) \to H_n(X)$ is an isomorphism.

proofs.name: Cellular model and presentations
proofs.slogan: Replace $X$ by a CW complex whose only cell below dimension $n$ is a point, and compare the presentations of $\pi_n$ and $H_n$ by cells.
proofs.scope: The case $n \ge 2$; the case $n = 1$, where $h$ induces $\pi_1(X)^{\mathrm{ab}} \cong H_1(X)$, is a separate statement with a different proof. Steps 4 and 5 use the excision theorem for homotopy groups, which needs $n \ge 2$ here.

roles.why: Connectivity lets the CW model have a single cell in all dimensions below $n$.
For $n \ge 2$, homotopy excision computes $\pi_n$ of a wedge of $n$-spheres and the effect of attaching $(n+1)$-cells.

steps.slogan: Replace $X$ by a [CW complex](c:cw-complex) through a weak homotopy equivalence.
steps.detail: CW approximation gives a CW complex $Z$ and a [weak homotopy equivalence](c:weak-homotopy-equivalence) $Z \to X$. It induces isomorphisms on homotopy groups and on singular homology and commutes with the Hurewicz maps, so it suffices to treat $Z$.

steps.slogan: Choose a model of $Z$ with one $0$-cell and no cells in dimensions $1$ to $n-1$.
steps.detail: Since $Z$ is $(n-1)$-connected, cellular approximation and the homotopy extension property give a homotopy equivalent CW complex whose $(n-1)$-skeleton is a point. Its [cellular homology](c:cellular-homology) gives $\tilde H_k(Z) = 0$ for $k < n$.

steps.slogan: Reduce $\pi_n$ and $H_n$ to the $(n+1)$-skeleton of the model.
steps.detail: Cellular approximation shows that the inclusion $Z^{n+1} \hookrightarrow Z$ is an isomorphism on $\pi_n$, and cellular homology shows the same for $H_n$. The Hurewicz maps commute with this inclusion.

steps.slogan: Compute $\pi_n$ of the $n$-skeleton, a [wedge sum](c:wedge-sum) of $n$-spheres.
steps.detail: The $n$-skeleton is $\bigvee_\alpha S^n_\alpha$. For $n \ge 2$, homotopy excision gives $\pi_n(\bigvee_\alpha S^n_\alpha) \cong \bigoplus_\alpha \mathbb{Z}$, generated by the inclusions of the spheres, and $h$ sends these generators to the basis of $H_n(\bigvee_\alpha S^n_\alpha) \cong \bigoplus_\alpha \mathbb{Z}$.

steps.slogan: Match the presentations of $\pi_n$ and $H_n$ after attaching the $(n+1)$-cells.
steps.detail: The exact sequence of the pair $(Z^{n+1}, Z^n)$ and homotopy excision show that $\pi_n(Z^{n+1})$ is $\pi_n(Z^n)$ modulo the classes of the attaching maps. Cellular homology shows that $H_n(Z^{n+1})$ is $H_n(Z^n)$ modulo the images of these classes under $h$, so $h$ is an isomorphism, and step 2 gives the rest.

concepts.c:n-connected-space: Connectivity removes all cells of the model below dimension $n$.
concepts.c:homology: Homology of the model is read off from its cellular chains.
concepts.c:homotopy-group: The proof presents $\pi_n$ by generators and relations from the cells.
concepts.c:cw-complex: The CW model has skeleta that the proof treats one at a time.
concepts.c:weak-homotopy-equivalence: It transfers the statement from $X$ to the CW model.
concepts.c:cellular-homology: Cellular chains present $H_n$ by $n$-cells modulo boundaries of $(n+1)$-cells.
concepts.c:wedge-sum: The $n$-skeleton is a wedge of spheres with known $\pi_n$.

source.note: The proof of Hatcher, Algebraic Topology (2002), theorem 4.32, through CW approximation, cellular approximation and the excision theorem for homotopy groups.

statement: Let $T$ be a [consistent](c:consistent-theory) theory whose axioms form a [recursive set](c:recursive-subset) and which proves the axioms of [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic). (1) Some arithmetic [sentence](c:sentence) is true in the natural numbers but not provable in $T$. (2) If $T$ contains [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic), then $T$ does not prove the sentence $\mathrm{Con}(T)$ that expresses its consistency.

hypotheses.text: The theory $T$ is [consistent](c:consistent-theory).
The axioms of $T$ form a [recursive set](c:recursive-subset).
The theory $T$ proves the axioms of [Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) $Q$.
For part (2), $T$ contains the axioms of [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic).

conclusion: Some true arithmetic sentence is unprovable in $T$, and under the hypothesis of part (2), $T \nvdash \mathrm{Con}(T)$.

proofs.name: Gödel sentence and its formalization
proofs.slogan: Build a sentence that says it is unprovable, check that it is true and unprovable, and formalize this check inside the theory.
proofs.scope: An outline of the published proof; the representability in step 1 and the derivability conditions in step 5 rest on the cited work. Part (1) needs only consistency because it claims truth in $\mathbb{N}$, not refutability of the negation.

roles.why: A recursive axiom set makes the proof relation recursive, so arithmetic represents it.
[Robinson arithmetic](c:robinson-arithmetic) represents recursive relations, proves the diagonal lemma and has only true theorems.
Consistency rules out a proof of the Gödel sentence.
[Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic) proves the derivability conditions that formalize step 3.

steps.slogan: Code formulas and proofs by numbers and define a provability formula.
steps.detail: A [Gödel numbering](c:godel-numbering) codes formulas and finite lists of formulas by numbers. Since the axioms form a recursive set, the relation that $p$ codes a $T$-proof of the formula with code $n$ is recursive, so a formula $\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, n)$ represents it in $Q$; set $\mathrm{Prov}_T(x) = \exists p\,\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, x)$.

steps.slogan: Build the Gödel sentence $G$ that states its own unprovability.
steps.detail: The diagonal lemma, provable in $Q$, gives a [sentence](c:sentence) $G$ with $Q \vdash G \leftrightarrow \neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$, so $G$ says that it has no proof in $T$.

steps.slogan: Show that the consistent theory $T$ does not prove $G$.
steps.detail: If $T \vdash G$ with a proof of code $p$, then $Q$ proves the true numerical instance $\mathrm{Prf}_T(p, \ulcorner G\urcorner)$, so $T \vdash \mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$ and step 2 gives $T \vdash \neg G$. That contradicts consistency.

steps.slogan: Check that $G$ is true in the natural numbers.
steps.detail: By step 3 no number codes a $T$-proof of $G$, so $\neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$ is true in $\mathbb{N}$. The theorems of $Q$ are true in $\mathbb{N}$, so the equivalence of step 2 holds there and $G$ is true.

steps.slogan: Formalize step 3 inside $T$ to prove $\mathrm{Con}(T) \to G$.
steps.detail: With Peano arithmetic, $T$ proves the Hilbert-Bernays-Löb derivability conditions for $\mathrm{Prov}_T$. They turn step 3 into a proof in $T$ of $\mathrm{Con}(T) \to \neg\mathrm{Prov}_T(\ulcorner G\urcorner)$, and step 2 turns it into $T \vdash \mathrm{Con}(T) \to G$.

steps.slogan: Combine the true unprovable sentence with the formalized implication.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give part (1). If $T \vdash \mathrm{Con}(T)$, step 5 gives $T \vdash G$, which step 3 excludes, so $T \nvdash \mathrm{Con}(T)$, which is part (2).

concepts.c:consistent-theory: Consistency is the only hypothesis that part (1) needs.
concepts.c:recursive-subset: A recursive axiom set makes proofs checkable by arithmetic formulas.
concepts.c:robinson-arithmetic: This weak true theory represents recursive relations and proves the diagonal lemma.
concepts.c:sentence: The unprovable statement is a single arithmetic sentence without free variables.
concepts.c:peano-arithmetic: Peano arithmetic proves the derivability conditions used for part (2).
concepts.c:godel-numbering: Numbering formulas lets an arithmetic sentence talk about its own proofs.

source.ref: P. Smith, An Introduction to Gödel's Theorems, 2nd edition, Cambridge University Press, Cambridge, 2013
source.note: Proves both theorems in this form, with the diagonal lemma and the derivability conditions. The original is K. Gödel, Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica und verwandter Systeme I, Monatshefte für Mathematik und Physik 38 (1931), 173-198, https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01700692.

statement: Let two lines meet at a point $S$, and let two distinct [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines) that avoid $S$ cut the first line at $A$ and $B$ and the second line at $A'$ and $B'$. Then $SA/SB = SA'/SB' = AA'/BB'$, so the [triangles](c:triangle) $SAA'$ and $SBB'$ have proportional sides.

hypotheses.text: Two distinct lines meet at the point $S$.
Two distinct [parallel lines](c:parallel-lines) avoid $S$; one cuts the given lines at $A$ and $A'$, the other at $B$ and $B'$.

proofs.name: Equal areas (Euclid)
proofs.slogan: Compare triangles on a common base between the parallels, then read the ratios of sides from the ratios of areas.
proofs.scope: The configuration with $A$ between $S$ and $B$; renaming the parallels covers $SB < SA$, and a point reflection through $S$ moves $A$ and $A'$ to the side of $B$ when $S$ lies between the parallels. Step 4 proves the third ratio from the first.

roles.why: The points $S, A, B$ and $S, A', B'$ lie on two lines, so triangles with a vertex off one line share a height.
Parallel lines keep a constant distance, so triangles on a base along one parallel with apexes on the other have equal heights.

steps.slogan: Show that the triangles $AA'B$ and $AA'B'$ have equal [area](c:area).
steps.detail: Both triangles have the base $AA'$. Their apexes $B$ and $B'$ lie on a line [parallel](c:parallel-lines) to $AA'$, so the two triangles have the same height over $AA'$ and the same area.

steps.slogan: Add the triangle $SAA'$ to both to get equal areas of $SBA'$ and $SAB'$.
steps.detail: Since $A$ lies on $SB$, the triangle $SBA'$ splits into $SAA'$ and $AA'B$. Since $A'$ lies on $SB'$, the triangle $SAB'$ splits into $SAA'$ and $AA'B'$, so step 1 gives $[SBA'] = [SAB']$.

steps.slogan: Divide the [area](c:area) of $SAA'$ by the two equal areas.
steps.detail: The triangles $SAA'$ and $SBA'$ have the same height from $A'$, so $[SAA']/[SBA'] = SA/SB$; the triangles $SAA'$ and $SAB'$ have the same height from $A$, so $[SAA']/[SAB'] = SA'/SB'$. Step 2 makes the denominators equal, so $SA/SB = SA'/SB'$.

steps.slogan: Draw through $A'$ a parallel to $SB$ to get the third ratio.
steps.detail: Let this parallel meet $BB'$ at $C$; then $ABCA'$ is a [parallelogram](c:parallelogram) and $BC = AA'$. Steps 1 to 3 at the vertex $B'$, with the parallels $A'C$ and $SB$, give $B'A'/B'S = B'C/B'B$, hence $SA'/SB' = CB/BB' = AA'/BB'$.

concepts.c:parallel-lines: Parallel lines give equal heights to triangles on a common base.
concepts.c:triangle: The proof compares areas of triangles with shared bases or heights.
concepts.c:area: Ratios of areas with a common height equal ratios of bases.
concepts.c:parallelogram: Opposite sides of the parallelogram move the length $AA'$ onto line $BB'$.

source.note: Euclid's proof by areas, Elements, book VI, proposition 2.

proofs.name: Vectors and linear independence
proofs.slogan: Write the four points as multiples of two independent vectors from $S$ and compare coefficients in the parallelism condition.
proofs.scope: All configurations at once, including $S$ between the parallels; the signed ratio $\lambda$ gives the length ratios as $|\lambda|$.

roles.why: Distinct lines through $S$ have [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) direction vectors.
Parallelism makes $A' - A$ a multiple of $B' - B$, and avoiding $S$ makes the coefficients nonzero.

steps.slogan: Place $S$ at the origin and write the points along two direction vectors.
steps.detail: Let $u$ and $v$ be direction vectors of the two lines; they are [linearly independent](c:linear-independence) because the lines are distinct. Then $A = au$, $B = bu$, $A' = a'v$ and $B' = b'v$ with nonzero reals $a, b, a', b'$, because the parallels avoid $S$.

steps.slogan: Express the parallelism of $AA'$ and $BB'$ by a real scalar $\lambda$.
steps.detail: Because the line $AA'$ is [parallel](c:parallel-lines) to the line $BB'$, some real number $\lambda$ satisfies $a'v - au = \lambda(b'v - bu)$.

steps.slogan: Compare the coefficients of $u$ and $v$ on both sides.
steps.detail: Linear independence of $u$ and $v$ gives $a = \lambda b$ and $a' = \lambda b'$. Hence $a/b = a'/b' = \lambda$, and $\lambda \ne 0$.

steps.slogan: Read the three ratios as the absolute value $|\lambda|$.
steps.detail: Now $SA/SB = |a|/|b| = |\lambda|$ and $SA'/SB' = |a'|/|b'| = |\lambda|$, and $A' - A = \lambda(B' - B)$ gives $AA'/BB' = |\lambda|$.

concepts.c:parallel-lines: Parallelism becomes the vector equation $A' - A = \lambda(B' - B)$.
concepts.c:triangle: The triangles $SAA'$ and $SBB'$ have sides in the ratio $|\lambda|$.
concepts.c:linear-independence: Independence of the two directions allows the comparison of coefficients.

source.note: The standard vector proof of the intercept theorem from analytic geometry.

statement: If $f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) and $y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$, then $f(c) = y$ for some $c \in [a, b]$.

hypotheses.text: The domain is a closed [interval](c:interval) $[a, b]$ with $a \le b$.
The function $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) on $[a, b]$.
The value $y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

formal.difference: The declaration states that the image of $[a, b]$ contains $[f(a), f(b)]$, for a densely ordered, conditionally complete domain and an order-closed codomain. The case $f(b) \le f(a)$ is the separate declaration intermediate_value_Icc'.

proofs.name: Connected image
proofs.slogan: The interval is connected, so its image is connected, and a connected set of reals contains every value between two of its values.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, for either order of $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.

roles.why: A closed [interval](c:interval) is a [connected space](c:connected-space).
A continuous map keeps connectedness.
The two end values are points of the image, and $y$ lies between them.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed interval $[a, b]$ is a [connected space](c:connected-space).
steps.detail: Suppose $[a, b] = U \cup V$ with disjoint nonempty relatively open sets and $a \in U$. Let $s = \sup\{x : [a, x] \subseteq U\}$. Openness of $U$ and of $V$ near $s$ gives a contradiction, so no such split exists.

steps.slogan: Push the connected interval forward to its connected [image](c:image) under $f$.
steps.detail: If $f([a, b])$ were split by two disjoint relatively open sets, their preimages under the [continuous](c:continuous-function) $f$ would split $[a, b]$, which step 1 excludes.

steps.slogan: Show that the connected image holds every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
steps.detail: If $y$ lies between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$ but is not a value, the sets $\{t < y\}$ and $\{t > y\}$ split the image into two nonempty relatively open parts, against step 2. So $y = f(c)$ for some $c$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity is what makes the image connected.
concepts.c:interval: The interval is the connected domain of the function.
concepts.c:connected-space: Connectedness is the property that passes from the domain to the image.
concepts.c:image: The proof studies the set of values $f([a, b])$.

proofs.name: Supremum of the lower set
proofs.slogan: Take the last point where $f$ is at most $y$ and show that $f$ equals $y$ there.
proofs.scope: The case $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$; the other case follows when the proof is applied to $-f$ and $-y$.

roles.why: The inequality $f(a) \le y$ puts $a$ in the set $S$, and $y \le f(b)$ controls the right end.
The bounded [interval](c:interval) makes $S$ bounded and keeps its supremum in $[a, b]$.
Continuity at $c$ passes both inequalities through the limits.

steps.slogan: Collect the points where $f$ stays at most $y$ into a set $S$.
steps.detail: Let $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) \le y\}$. Because $f(a) \le y$, the point $a$ is in $S$, so $S$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Take the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) $c$ of the nonempty bounded set $S$.
steps.detail: The set $S$ is nonempty and bounded above by $b$, so the completeness of the [real numbers](c:real-number) gives $c = \sup S$, and $a \le c \le b$.

steps.slogan: Approach $c$ from inside $S$ to get $f(c) \le y$.
steps.detail: Choose $x_n \in S$ with $x_n \to c$. Then $f(x_n) \le y$ and [continuity](c:continuous-function) gives $f(c) = \lim f(x_n) \le y$.

steps.slogan: Approach $c$ from the right to get $f(c) \ge y$.
steps.detail: If $c = b$, then $f(c) = f(b) \ge y$. If $c < b$, the points $c + 1/n$ (for large $n$) are not in $S$, so $f(c + 1/n) > y$, and continuity gives $f(c) \ge y$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inequalities into $f(c) = y$.
steps.detail: Steps 3 and 4 give $y \le f(c) \le y$, so $f(c) = y$ with $c \in [a, b]$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at the supremum turns limits of inequalities into inequalities.
concepts.c:interval: The interval bounds the set $S$ and holds its supremum.
concepts.c:least-upper-bound: The supremum of $S$ is the point where $f$ meets $y$.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals supplies the supremum.

source.note: The classical least-upper-bound proof (Bolzano's proof as usually taught).

proofs.name: Bisection
proofs.slogan: Halve the interval again and again, keep a half whose end values straddle $y$, and take the common point.
proofs.scope: The case $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$; the other case follows from $-f$ and $-y$.

roles.why: The first interval has $f(a) \le y \le f(b)$, which starts the halving.
A closed bounded [interval](c:interval) can be halved into closed intervals whose lengths go to zero.
Continuity at the common point passes both end inequalities to the limit.

steps.slogan: Halve the current interval and keep a half whose end values straddle $y$.
steps.detail: Given $[a_n, b_n]$ with $f(a_n) \le y \le f(b_n)$, let $m$ be its midpoint. If $f(m) \le y$, keep $[m, b_n]$; otherwise keep $[a_n, m]$. The kept half has the same property.

steps.slogan: Repeat the halving to get nested intervals of length $(b - a)/2^n$.
steps.detail: The intervals $[a_n, b_n]$ are nested, $a_n$ increases, $b_n$ decreases and $b_n - a_n = (b - a)/2^n \to 0$.

steps.slogan: Take the common point $c$ of the nested intervals.
steps.detail: The bounded monotone sequences $a_n$ and $b_n$ converge in the [real numbers](c:real-number) to the same limit $c \in [a, b]$.

steps.slogan: Pass to the limit at both ends to get $f(c) = y$.
steps.detail: By [continuity](c:continuous-function), $f(c) = \lim f(a_n) \le y$ and $f(c) = \lim f(b_n) \ge y$, so $f(c) = y$.

concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity at the common point turns the end inequalities into an equation.
concepts.c:interval: Closed intervals can be halved and nested.
concepts.c:real-number: Completeness of the reals gives the common point of the nested intervals.

source.note: The bisection proof, which is also the bisection method for root finding.

statement: Let $V$ be a [finite-dimensional vector space](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space) over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) $K$ and $f$ an endomorphism of $V$. Then $f = n + s$, where $n$ is a [nilpotent endomorphism](c:nilpotent-endomorphism), $s$ is a [semisimple endomorphism](c:semisimple-endomorphism), and both are polynomials in $f$, so they commute.

hypotheses.text: The vector space $V$ is [finite-dimensional](c:finite-dimensional-vector-space).
The field $K$ is [perfect](c:perfect-field).

conclusion: Some $n, s \in K[f]$ satisfy $f = n + s$ with $n$ nilpotent and $s$ semisimple.

proofs.name: Newton iteration in K[f]
proofs.slogan: Find a root $s$ of the squarefree part of the minimal polynomial close to $f$ by Newton's method in the commutative algebra $K[f]$.
proofs.scope: Existence only; uniqueness is a separate result. For $V = 0$ the choice $n = s = 0$ works.

roles.why: Finite dimension makes the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $f$ nonzero.
Over a perfect field the squarefree part $g$ is separable, so $g'$ is invertible modulo $g$.

steps.slogan: Take the squarefree part $g$ of the [minimal polynomial](c:minimal-polynomial) of $f$.
steps.detail: The minimal polynomial $\mu$ of $f$ is nonzero because $V$ is finite-dimensional. Let $g$ be the product of its distinct monic irreducible factors; then $g$ is [squarefree](c:square-free-polynomial) and $\mu \mid g^k$ for some $k$, so $g(f)^k = 0$.

steps.slogan: Invert $g'(t)$ in $K[f]$ whenever $g(t)$ is nilpotent, by separability of $g$.
steps.detail: Over a [perfect field](c:perfect-field) every irreducible polynomial is separable, so the squarefree $g$ is coprime to $g'$ and $a g' + b g^k = 1$ for some polynomials $a, b$. For $t \in K[f]$ with $g(t)$ nilpotent, $a(t) g'(t) = 1 - b(t) g(t)^k$ is a unit, so $g'(t)$ is a unit.

steps.slogan: Run [Newton's iteration](c:newton-s-method) $s_{j+1} = s_j - g(s_j)\,g'(s_j)^{-1}$ from $s_0 = f$.
steps.detail: By induction each $g(s_j)$ is [nilpotent](c:nilpotent-element), so $g'(s_j)$ is a unit by step 2. Taylor expansion of $g$ at $s_j$ gives $g(s_{j+1}) \in g(s_j)^2 K[f]$, and $s_{j+1} - s_j \in g(s_j) K[f]$ is nilpotent.

steps.slogan: Stop once $2^j \ge k$ to get $g(s) = 0$ with $f - s$ nilpotent.
steps.detail: Step 3 gives $g(s_j) \in g(f)^{2^j} K[f]$, which is $0$ once $2^j \ge k$; let $s = s_j$. The difference $f - s$ is a sum of nilpotent elements of the commutative ring $K[f]$, so it is nilpotent.

steps.slogan: Show that $s$ is semisimple and set $n = f - s$.
steps.detail: The minimal polynomial of $s$ divides the squarefree $g$, so $K[s]$ is a product of fields by the Chinese remainder theorem and $s$ is [semisimple](c:semisimple-endomorphism). Then $n = f - s$ is a [nilpotent endomorphism](c:nilpotent-endomorphism), both lie in $K[f]$, and $f = n + s$.

concepts.c:finite-dimensional-vector-space: Finite dimension gives a nonzero minimal polynomial.
concepts.c:perfect-field: Perfectness makes the squarefree part separable for Newton's method.
concepts.c:nilpotent-endomorphism: The nilpotent part is the Newton correction $f - s$.
concepts.c:semisimple-endomorphism: The Newton limit $s$ is semisimple because a squarefree polynomial kills it.
concepts.c:minimal-polynomial: Its squarefree part is the polynomial whose root $s$ the proof seeks.
concepts.c:square-free-polynomial: A squarefree annihilating polynomial makes an endomorphism semisimple.
concepts.c:nilpotent-element: Nilpotent errors vanish after finitely many Newton steps.
concepts.c:newton-s-method: Newton's iteration squares the error at each step.

statement: Let $E$ be a real Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) and $K \subseteq E$ a [compact](c:compact-space) [convex set](c:convex-set). Then $K$ is the closure of the [convex hull](c:convex-hull) of the set of [extreme points](c:extreme-point) of $K$.

hypotheses.text: The space $E$ is a real Hausdorff [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space).
The set $K$ is [compact](c:compact-space).
The set $K$ is [convex](c:convex-set).

proofs.name: Separation and an exposed face
proofs.slogan: Separate a missing point from the closed convex hull by a functional, and find an extreme point where this functional is largest.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $K = \emptyset$ both sides are empty. Step 4 uses the Krein-Milman lemma, which gives an extreme point of a nonempty compact set by Zorn's lemma.

roles.why: Local convexity gives the separating continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional), and the Hausdorff property makes $K$ closed.
Compactness makes $K$ closed, lets the functional attain its maximum, and makes the maximizing face compact.
Convexity keeps the convex hull of the extreme points inside $K$.

steps.slogan: Show that the closed convex hull $C$ of the extreme points lies in $K$.
steps.detail: The [extreme points](c:extreme-point) lie in the [convex](c:convex-set) set $K$, so their [convex hull](c:convex-hull) lies in $K$. A compact set in a Hausdorff space is closed, so the closure $C$ of this hull lies in $K$.

steps.slogan: Separate a point $x \in K \setminus C$ from $C$ by a continuous linear functional.
steps.detail: Suppose $x \in K$ is not in the closed convex set $C$. The Hahn-Banach separation theorem in the [locally convex space](c:locally-convex-space) gives a continuous [linear functional](c:linear-functional) $l$ and a real $r$ with $l < r$ on $C$ and $l(x) > r$.

steps.slogan: Take the face $F$ of $K$ where $l$ attains its maximum.
steps.detail: The continuous $l$ attains a maximum $M$ on the nonempty [compact](c:compact-space) $K$, and $M \ge l(x) > r$. The set $F = \{y \in K : l(y) = M\}$ is nonempty and compact, and it is a face: a segment of $K$ with an interior point in $F$ lies in $F$.

steps.slogan: Find an extreme point of $F$ and check that it is extreme in $K$.
steps.detail: The nonempty compact set $F$ has an extreme point $y$ by the Krein-Milman lemma. Because $F$ is a face of $K$, the point $y$ is also an extreme point of $K$, so $y \in C$.

steps.slogan: Compare the two values of $l$ at $y$ to get a contradiction.
steps.detail: Since $y \in C$, step 2 gives $l(y) < r$, and since $y \in F$, step 3 gives $l(y) = M > r$. This contradiction shows $K \subseteq C$, so $K = C$ by step 1.

concepts.c:locally-convex-space: Local convexity supplies functionals that separate points from closed convex sets.
concepts.c:compact-space: Compactness gives the maximum of $l$ and the compact face.
concepts.c:convex-set: Convexity keeps the hull of the extreme points inside $K$.
concepts.c:convex-hull: The closed convex hull is the set that the theorem identifies with $K$.
concepts.c:extreme-point: The extreme point found on the maximizing face breaks the separation.
concepts.c:linear-functional: The separating functional detects the missing point and defines the face.

statement: Let $R$ be a commutative [Noetherian ring](c:noetherian-ring) and $I = (x)$ a [principal ideal](c:principal-ideal). Then every [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $\mathfrak p$ that is minimal among the prime ideals containing $I$ has [height](c:height) at most $1$.

hypotheses.text: The commutative ring $R$ is [Noetherian](c:noetherian-ring).
The ideal $I = (x)$ is [principal](c:principal-ideal).
The [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal) $\mathfrak p$ is minimal among the prime ideals that contain $I$.

conclusion: $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p \le 1$: no chain of primes $\mathfrak q' \subsetneq \mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ exists.

proofs.name: Artinian quotient and symbolic powers
proofs.slogan: Localize at $\mathfrak p$, make $R/(x)$ Artinian, and show that the symbolic powers of a smaller prime stabilize, which forces that prime to have height zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; if $x$ is a unit, no prime contains $I$ and the statement is empty. The proof shows that every prime $\mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ has height $0$.

roles.why: Noetherianity makes $R_{\mathfrak p}/(x)$ Artinian and keeps the ideals finitely generated for Nakayama's lemma.
A single generator $x$ lets a relation $y = z + ax$ be solved for $a$.
Minimality makes $\mathfrak p$ the only prime over $(x)$ after localization, and it keeps $x$ out of every smaller prime.

steps.slogan: Localize at $\mathfrak p$ to make $\mathfrak p$ the maximal ideal of a local ring.
steps.detail: The [localization](c:localization-of-a-ring) $R_{\mathfrak p}$ is Noetherian and local, its primes match the primes of $R$ inside $\mathfrak p$ with the same heights, and $\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}$ is minimal over $xR_{\mathfrak p}$. So assume that $R$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p$.

steps.slogan: Show that the quotient ring $R/(x)$ is Artinian.
steps.detail: By minimality, $\mathfrak p$ is the only prime that contains $x$, so the Noetherian ring $R/(x)$ has [Krull dimension](c:krull-dimension) $0$. A Noetherian ring of dimension $0$ is [Artinian](c:artinian-ring).

steps.slogan: Stabilize the symbolic powers of a prime $\mathfrak q \subsetneq \mathfrak p$ modulo $x$.
steps.detail: Let $\mathfrak q^{(n)} = \mathfrak q^nR_{\mathfrak q} \cap R$. The ideals $(\mathfrak q^{(n)} + (x))/(x)$ of $R/(x)$ decrease, so the Artinian property gives $n$ with $\mathfrak q^{(n)} \subseteq \mathfrak q^{(n+1)} + (x)$.

steps.slogan: Deduce $\mathfrak q^{(n)} = \mathfrak q^{(n+1)}$ from the single generator and Nakayama's lemma.
steps.detail: If $y \in \mathfrak q^{(n)}$ and $y = z + ax$ with $z \in \mathfrak q^{(n+1)}$, then $ax \in \mathfrak q^{(n)}$ and $x \notin \mathfrak q$, so $a \in \mathfrak q^{(n)}$. Hence $\mathfrak q^{(n)} = \mathfrak q^{(n+1)} + x\mathfrak q^{(n)}$, and Nakayama's lemma with $x \in \mathfrak p$ gives $\mathfrak q^{(n)} = \mathfrak q^{(n+1)}$.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $\mathfrak qR_{\mathfrak q}$ is nilpotent, so $\mathfrak q$ has height $0$.
steps.detail: Localization gives $\mathfrak q^nR_{\mathfrak q} = \mathfrak q^{n+1}R_{\mathfrak q}$, and Nakayama's lemma in the local ring $R_{\mathfrak q}$ gives $\mathfrak q^nR_{\mathfrak q} = 0$. So $R_{\mathfrak q}$ has dimension $0$, every prime strictly inside $\mathfrak p$ is minimal, and $\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p \le 1$.

concepts.c:noetherian-ring: Noetherianity gives the Artinian quotient and finitely generated ideals.
concepts.c:principal-ideal: One generator allows the cancellation of $x$ in step 4.
concepts.c:prime-ideal: Chains of prime ideals below $\mathfrak p$ define its height.
concepts.c:height: The height of $\mathfrak p$ is the quantity that the theorem bounds.
concepts.c:localization-of-a-ring: Localization makes $\mathfrak p$ maximal and keeps the heights.
concepts.c:krull-dimension: Dimension zero of $R/(x)$ makes it Artinian.
concepts.c:artinian-ring: The descending chain condition stabilizes the symbolic powers modulo $x$.

statement: Let $X$ be a nonempty [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) and $f\colon X \to X$ a [continuous](c:continuous-function) map. Then $X$ carries a [regular](c:regular-measure) Borel [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $\mu$ that is an [invariant measure](c:invariant-measure) of $f$: $\mu(f^{-1}(A)) = \mu(A)$ for every Borel set $A$.

hypotheses.text: The space $X$ is nonempty.
The space $X$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space) with its Borel sets.
The map $f\colon X \to X$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function).

conclusion: Some regular Borel probability measure $\mu$ on $X$ satisfies $f_*\mu = \mu$.

proofs.name: Cluster point of empirical measures
proofs.slogan: Average the point masses along an orbit, take a cluster point of these averages, and check that the defect of invariance tends to zero.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. Nonemptiness supplies the starting point of the orbit; on the empty space no probability measure exists.

roles.why: A point $x \in X$ starts the orbit that defines the averages.
Compactness makes the probability measures weak-* compact and gives a regular measure that represents the limit functional.
Continuity makes $g \circ f$ continuous, so invariance can be tested on continuous functions.

steps.slogan: Average the point masses along the orbit of a point $x$.
steps.detail: Fix $x \in X$ and set $\mu_n = \frac1n \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \delta_{f^k(x)}$. Each $\mu_n$ is a Borel [probability measure](c:probability-measure) with $\int g\,d\mu_n = \frac1n \sum_{k<n} g(f^k(x))$.

steps.slogan: Bound the defect of invariance of $\mu_n$ by a telescoping sum.
steps.detail: For continuous $g\colon X \to \mathbb{R}$ the inner terms cancel in $\int g \circ f\,d\mu_n - \int g\,d\mu_n = \frac1n (g(f^n(x)) - g(x))$. Its absolute value is at most $2\|g\|_\infty/n$, which tends to $0$.

steps.slogan: Take a cluster point of the averages by [weak-* compactness](c:weak-compactness-2).
steps.detail: The positive functionals of norm $1$ on $C(X)$ form a weak-* closed subset of the unit ball of $C(X)^*$, which is weak-* compact by the Banach-Alaoglu theorem. So the sequence $(\mu_n)$, viewed as functionals, has a cluster point $\Lambda$, a positive functional with $\Lambda(1) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Represent the cluster point by a regular Borel probability measure $\mu$.
steps.detail: The Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem gives a [regular](c:regular-measure) Borel measure $\mu$ with $\int g\,d\mu = \Lambda(g)$ for all continuous $g$. Testing $g = 1$ gives $\mu(X) = 1$.

steps.slogan: Pass the vanishing defect to $\mu$ and identify $f_*\mu$ with $\mu$.
steps.detail: Step 2 and the cluster point property give $\int g\,d(f_*\mu) = \int g \circ f\,d\mu = \int g\,d\mu$ for every continuous $g$. The pushforward $f_*\mu$ is again regular, and the uniqueness in the Riesz-Markov-Kakutani theorem makes $\mu$ an [invariant measure](c:invariant-measure).

concepts.c:compact-hausdorff-space: Compact Hausdorff spaces have the Riesz representation of positive functionals.
concepts.c:continuous-function: Continuity keeps $g \circ f$ a valid test function.
concepts.c:regular-measure: Regularity makes a measure determined by its integrals of continuous functions.
concepts.c:probability-measure: The empirical averages and their limit are probability measures.
concepts.c:invariant-measure: Invariance is the property that the cluster point inherits.
concepts.c:weak-compactness-2: Weak-* compactness supplies the cluster point of the averages.

statement: Let $R$ be a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain) and $X, Y$ topological spaces. For every $n$ there is a natural short [exact sequence](c:exact-sequence) of singular [homology](c:homology) groups with coefficients in $R$, $0 \to \bigoplus_{i+j=n} H_i(X) \otimes_R H_j(Y) \to H_n(X \times Y) \to \bigoplus_{i+j=n-1} \operatorname{Tor}^R_1(H_i(X), H_j(Y)) \to 0$, built from the [tensor product](c:tensor-product), the cross product and the [Tor functor](c:tor-functor); it splits, but not naturally.

hypotheses.text: The coefficient ring $R$ is a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain).

conclusion: The sequence is exact and splits, so $H_n(X \times Y;R)$ is the direct sum of the tensor terms and the Tor terms.

proofs.name: Eilenberg-Zilber and algebraic Künneth
proofs.slogan: Replace the chains of the product by a tensor product of chain complexes, then compute its homology over the principal ideal domain.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, in every degree $n \ge 0$; the splitting is not natural. If $X$ or $Y$ is empty, all groups are $0$ and the sequence is trivially exact.

roles.why: Over a PID submodules of free modules are free, so cycles and boundaries are free and the needed sequences split.

steps.slogan: Replace $C_*(X \times Y)$ by $C_*(X) \otimes_R C_*(Y)$ through the Eilenberg-Zilber equivalence.
steps.detail: The Eilenberg-Zilber theorem, proved by acyclic models, gives a natural [chain homotopy equivalence](c:chain-homotopy-equivalence) $C_*(X;R) \otimes_R C_*(Y;R) \to C_*(X \times Y;R)$ that induces the cross product. So $H_n(X \times Y;R)$ is the homology of the complex $C \otimes D$ with $C = C_*(X;R)$ and $D = C_*(Y;R)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the cycles and boundaries of the complex $C$ are free modules.
steps.detail: Each $C_n$ is a [free module](c:free-module) over $R$ on the singular simplices. Over a principal ideal domain, submodules of free modules are free, so the cycles $Z_n$ and the boundaries $B_n$ are free.

steps.slogan: Tensor the sequence $0 \to Z \to C \to B[-1] \to 0$ with the complex $D$.
steps.detail: The sequence $0 \to Z_n \to C_n \to B_{n-1} \to 0$ splits because $B_{n-1}$ is free, so it stays exact after tensoring with $D$. Since $Z$ and $B$ are free with zero differentials, $H(Z \otimes D) = Z \otimes H(D)$ and $H(B \otimes D) = B \otimes H(D)$.

steps.slogan: Read the long exact homology sequence, whose connecting map comes from $B \hookrightarrow Z$.
steps.detail: The long exact sequence links $(B \otimes H(D))_n$, $(Z \otimes H(D))_n$, $H_n(C \otimes D)$ and $(B \otimes H(D))_{n-1}$, and its connecting maps are $i \otimes 1$ for the inclusion $i\colon B \to Z$. So $H_n(C \otimes D)$ is an extension of $\ker(i \otimes 1)$ in degree $n-1$ by $\operatorname{coker}(i \otimes 1)$ in degree $n$.

steps.slogan: Identify the kernel and cokernel of $i \otimes 1$ by the free resolution of $H(C)$.
steps.detail: Tensoring the free resolution $0 \to B \to Z \to H(C) \to 0$ with $H(D)$ gives $\operatorname{coker}(i \otimes 1) = H(C) \otimes H(D)$ and $\ker(i \otimes 1) = \operatorname{Tor}_1^R(H(C), H(D))$, degree by degree. This gives the exact sequence for $C \otimes D$, with the cross product as its first map.

steps.slogan: Split the sequence by retractions of the chain modules onto the cycles.
steps.detail: Because the boundaries are free, there are retractions $p\colon C \to Z$ and $q\colon D \to Z(D)$. The map $c \otimes d \mapsto [p(c)] \otimes [q(d)]$ kills boundaries, so it induces a left inverse $H(C \otimes D) \to H(C) \otimes H(D)$ of the first map, and step 1 moves the split sequence to $X \times Y$.

concepts.c:principal-ideal-domain: Over a PID submodules of free modules are free, which drives the algebra.
concepts.c:exact-sequence: The answer is a split short exact sequence read from a long one.
concepts.c:homology: The homology of the product comes from the homology of the factors.
concepts.c:tensor-product: The tensor product of chain complexes models the chains of the product.
concepts.c:tor-functor: Tor is the kernel of $i \otimes 1$ computed from the free resolution.
concepts.c:chain-homotopy-equivalence: The Eilenberg-Zilber map is one, so it preserves homology.
concepts.c:free-module: Free chain, cycle and boundary modules keep the tensored sequences exact.

statement: Let $T$ be an infinite [rooted tree](c:rooted-tree) in which every vertex has only finitely many children. Then $T$ has an infinite [path](c:path) $v_0 v_1 v_2 \dots$ that starts at the root and in which each $v_{i+1}$ is a child of $v_i$.

hypotheses.text: The tree $T$ has [infinitely many](c:infinite-set) vertices.
Every vertex of $T$ has only [finitely many](c:finite-set) children.

conclusion: Some infinite sequence $v_0, v_1, \dots$ starts at the root and has $v_{i+1}$ a child of $v_i$ for every $i$.

formal.difference: The declaration works in a strongly atomic partial order in which each element has finitely many covers and b has infinitely many elements above it, and it gives a sequence from b in which each term covers the previous one. A rooted tree ordered by ancestry is such an order, with covers equal to children.

proofs.name: Always step into an infinite subtree
proofs.slogan: Move from each vertex with infinitely many descendants to a child with the same property, which exists by the pigeonhole principle.
proofs.scope: The whole lemma; the path is built by a recursion that makes countably many dependent choices.

roles.why: The root then has infinitely many descendants, which starts the recursion.
Finitely many children split an infinite set of descendants into finitely many parts, so one part is infinite.

steps.slogan: Order the tree by ancestry and split the descendants of a vertex by its children.
steps.detail: Write $u \le w$ when $u$ lies on the path from the root to $w$; this is a [partial order](c:partial-order) whose covers are the parent-child pairs. Let $D(u)$ be the set of descendants of $u$, with $u$ included; every $w \in D(u)$ other than $u$ lies in $D(c)$ for the child $c$ of $u$ on the path to $w$.

steps.slogan: Note that the root has infinitely many descendants.
steps.detail: Every vertex of $T$ is a descendant of the root $r$, so $D(r) = T$ is an [infinite set](c:infinite-set) by hypothesis.

steps.slogan: Find a child $c$ of a vertex $u$ with $D(u)$ infinite such that $D(c)$ is infinite.
steps.detail: By step 1, $D(u) = \{u\} \cup D(c_1) \cup \dots \cup D(c_m)$ for the children $c_1, \dots, c_m$ of $u$, and $m$ is finite. A finite union of [finite sets](c:finite-set) is finite, so some $D(c_i)$ is infinite.

steps.slogan: Choose the children one by one to build the infinite path.
steps.detail: Set $v_0 = r$, and given $v_i$ with $D(v_i)$ infinite, let $v_{i+1}$ be a child given by step 3. Recursion with [dependent choice](c:dependent-choice) gives an infinite sequence with $v_{i+1}$ a child of $v_i$ for every $i$.

concepts.c:rooted-tree: The root and the child relation of the tree define the path.
concepts.c:path: The infinite path is the object that the lemma produces.
concepts.c:infinite-set: Infinitely many descendants is the property kept at every step.
concepts.c:finite-set: Finitely many children make the subtrees finitely many.
concepts.c:partial-order: Ancestry is the order in which mathlib states the lemma.
concepts.c:dependent-choice: Countably many dependent choices build the path.

statement: Let $s$ be a finite [signed measure](c:signed-measure) and $\mu$ a [σ-finite measure](c:sigma-finite-measure) on a measurable space $(\alpha, \mathcal M)$. Then $s = t + f\mu$, where $t$ is a signed measure that is [singular](c:singular-measure) with respect to $\mu$, $f$ is a $\mu$-[integrable function](c:integrable-function), and $(f\mu)(E) = \int_E f\,d\mu$.

hypotheses.text: The set function $s$ is a finite [signed measure](c:signed-measure) on $\mathcal M$.
The measure $\mu$ is [σ-finite](c:sigma-finite-measure).

conclusion: Some signed measure $t \perp \mu$ and some $f \in L^1(\mu)$ satisfy $s = t + f\mu$.

formal.difference: The declaration assumes the class HaveLebesgueDecomposition (both Jordan parts of $s$ decompose with respect to $\mu$), which mathlib provides for σ-finite $\mu$. It states the identity for the named choices singularPart and rnDeriv, whose singularity and integrability are separate lemmas.

proofs.name: Decompose the Jordan parts
proofs.slogan: Split $s$ into its positive and negative parts, decompose each finite measure with respect to $\mu$, and subtract the two decompositions.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; for $s = 0$ the proof gives $t = 0$ and $f = 0$.

roles.why: A finite signed measure has a [Jordan decomposition](c:jordan-decomposition) into two finite measures.
σ-finiteness of $\mu$ gives the Lebesgue decomposition of each finite measure.

steps.slogan: Split $s$ into two finite measures by the [Jordan decomposition](c:jordan-decomposition).
steps.detail: The Hahn decomposition gives a measurable set $P$ with $s \ge 0$ on the subsets of $P$ and $s \le 0$ on the subsets of its complement. Then $s^+ = s(\cdot \cap P)$ and $s^- = -s(\cdot \setminus P)$ are finite measures with $s = s^+ - s^-$.

steps.slogan: Decompose each part as a singular measure plus a density with respect to $\mu$.
steps.detail: The Lebesgue decomposition theorem for the σ-finite $\mu$ gives $s^\pm = \nu^\pm + g^\pm\mu$ with $\nu^\pm \perp \mu$ and measurable $g^\pm \ge 0$. The density parts come from the Radon-Nikodym theorem.

steps.slogan: Show that the densities $g^\pm$ are integrable and the measures $\nu^\pm$ finite.
steps.detail: The inequalities $\int g^\pm\,d\mu \le s^\pm(\alpha) < \infty$ and $\nu^\pm(\alpha) \le s^\pm(\alpha)$ hold. So $g^\pm$ are [integrable](c:integrable-function) and $\nu^\pm$ are finite measures.

steps.slogan: Show that $t = \nu^+ - \nu^-$ is [singular](c:singular-measure) with respect to $\mu$.
steps.detail: Choose $\mu$-null sets $N^\pm$ on which $\nu^\pm$ are concentrated. Then the finite signed measure $t$ is concentrated on the $\mu$-null set $N^+ \cup N^-$, so $t \perp \mu$.

steps.slogan: Subtract the two decompositions to get $s = t + f\mu$.
steps.detail: Set $f = g^+ - g^-$, which is integrable. Linearity of $g \mapsto g\mu$ on integrable functions gives $s = s^+ - s^- = (\nu^+ - \nu^-) + (g^+ - g^-)\mu = t + f\mu$.

concepts.c:signed-measure: The signed measure is the object that the proof decomposes.
concepts.c:sigma-finite-measure: σ-finiteness is what the Lebesgue decomposition of measures needs.
concepts.c:singular-measure: The singular part lives on a $\mu$-null set.
concepts.c:integrable-function: An integrable density makes $f\mu$ a finite signed measure.
concepts.c:jordan-decomposition: It reduces the signed case to two finite measures.

statement: Let $M$ be a compact oriented [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary and $f\colon M \to M$ a smooth map with $\det(I - df_x) \ne 0$ at every fixed point $x$. Then $\sum_{f(x) = x} \operatorname{sign}\det(I - df_x) = L(f)$, where the [Lefschetz number](c:lefschetz-number) $L(f) = \sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{tr}(f_*|H_k(M;\mathbb{Q}))$ is the alternating sum of the [traces](c:trace-of-a-matrix) on rational [homology](c:homology).

hypotheses.text: The space $M$ is a compact oriented [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) without boundary.
The map $f\colon M \to M$ is smooth.
At every [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $x$ of $f$, $\det(I - df_x) \ne 0$.

conclusion: The fixed points of $f$, counted with the signs $\operatorname{sign}\det(I - df_x)$, add up to $L(f)$.

proofs.name: Graph meets diagonal
proofs.slogan: Write $L(f)$ as the intersection number of the graph of $f$ with the diagonal, and compute this number locally at the fixed points.
proofs.scope: The whole formula; when $f$ has no fixed points, both sides are $0$. The orientation serves Poincaré duality only, because the local signs do not depend on it.

roles.why: Orientation gives Poincaré duality on $M \times M$, and compactness makes the fixed points finitely many.
Smoothness makes the graph $\Gamma_f$ a submanifold with tangent spaces given by $df_x$.
Nondegeneracy is exactly the [transversality](c:transversality) of the graph and the diagonal.

steps.slogan: Compute the [intersection number](c:intersection-number) of the graph and the diagonal by Poincaré duality.
steps.detail: Let $\Gamma_f = \{(x, f(x))\}$ and $\Delta = \{(x, x)\}$ in $M \times M$. Write the Poincaré dual of $\Delta$ by the Künneth formula in a basis of $H^*(M;\mathbb{Q})$ and its dual basis for the [cup product](c:cup-product) pairing; pulling it back along $x \mapsto (x, f(x))$ and integrating gives $\Gamma_f \cdot \Delta = \sum_k (-1)^k \operatorname{tr}(f^*|H^k(M;\mathbb{Q}))$.

steps.slogan: Replace the traces on cohomology by the traces on homology.
steps.detail: Over $\mathbb{Q}$ the space $H^k(M;\mathbb{Q})$ is the dual of $H_k(M;\mathbb{Q})$, and $f^*$ is the transpose of $f_*$. A transpose has the same [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix), so $\Gamma_f \cdot \Delta = L(f)$.

steps.slogan: Show that the graph meets the diagonal transversally in finitely many points.
steps.detail: At a [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $x$, the tangent spaces $\{(v, df_x v)\}$ of $\Gamma_f$ and $\{(w, w)\}$ of $\Delta$ span $T_xM \oplus T_xM$ exactly when $I - df_x$ is invertible. So the intersection is [transverse](c:transversality), its points are isolated, and compactness makes them finitely many.

steps.slogan: Compute the local intersection sign at a fixed point as $\operatorname{sign}\det(I - df_x)$.
steps.detail: Oriented bases of the two tangent spaces, written in an oriented basis of $T_xM \oplus T_xM$, form the block matrix with rows $(I, I)$ and $(A, I)$ for $A = df_x$. Its determinant is $\det(I - A)$, so the point contributes $\operatorname{sign}\det(I - df_x)$.

steps.slogan: Add the local signs to get the intersection number and hence $L(f)$.
steps.detail: For a transverse intersection of compact oriented submanifolds of complementary dimensions, the intersection number is the sum of the local signs. Steps 1 to 4 give $\sum_{f(x)=x} \operatorname{sign}\det(I - df_x) = \Gamma_f \cdot \Delta = L(f)$.

concepts.c:smooth-manifold: The graph and the diagonal are submanifolds of $M \times M$.
concepts.c:lefschetz-number: The homological side of the formula is the Lefschetz number.
concepts.c:trace-of-a-matrix: Traces of the induced maps appear when the diagonal class is pulled back.
concepts.c:homology: Rational homology supplies the traces on the right side.
concepts.c:fixed-point: Fixed points are the intersection points of the graph and the diagonal.
concepts.c:transversality: Transversality turns the intersection number into a finite signed count.
concepts.c:intersection-number: The intersection number joins the global side and the local side.
concepts.c:cup-product: The cup product pairing gives the dual basis for the diagonal class.

source.note: The intersection-theoretic proof through the Poincaré dual of the diagonal, as in Griffiths and Harris, Principles of Algebraic Geometry (1978), chapter 3, the section on fixed-point formulas.
